concepts.caption: The money the company actually made, reported quarterly or annually.
concepts.definition: Net profit after all costs over a period — the headline number of a results release.
concepts.example: BP posted a second-quarter profit that more than doubled to $5.73 billion.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Earnings are what is left after costs; revenue is the top line before any costs come out.

concepts.caption: Money taken in from sales, before a single cost is deducted.
concepts.definition: Total income from selling goods or services, also called the top line.
concepts.example: Revenue beat estimates at $21.4 billion.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Revenue is the gross take; earnings are what survives the costs.

concepts.caption: What is left after every cost comes out.
concepts.definition: The amount remaining after all costs and expenses are deducted from revenue.
concepts.example: The company reported its strongest quarterly profit in at least six years.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Profit is an amount; margin is the share of revenue it represents. Revenue can double while profit goes nowhere if the margin halves.

concepts.caption: After direct costs only — before admin, sales, interest and tax.
concepts.definition: Profit or margin after deducting direct production costs, excluding period expenses.
concepts.example: Gross margin expanded 180 basis points to 34%.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Gross stops at direct costs; net deducts everything, including interest and tax.

concepts.caption: Everything has been deducted.
concepts.definition: The amount after all costs, expenses, interest and tax.
concepts.example: Net income was flat excluding one-off items.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Net is the last figure standing; gross only cleared the first layer.

concepts.caption: Net profit spread across each share.
concepts.definition: Net profit divided by shares outstanding, letting you compare companies of different sizes.
concepts.example: Chevron reported adjusted earnings of $6.06 per share.
concepts.mixUpWhy: EPS is divided by share count; earnings is the whole. Same profit with a different share count gives a very different EPS.

concepts.caption: How much of each dollar of sales survives as profit.
concepts.definition: Profit as a percentage of revenue — profitability, not size.
concepts.example: Gross margin expanded 180 basis points to 34%.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Margin is a ratio; profit is an amount. Double the revenue at half the margin and profit barely moves.

concepts.caption: Forces pushing results back.
concepts.definition: External factors that hurt performance: higher costs, adverse currency moves, weaker demand.
concepts.example: Earnings per share missed consensus on higher headwinds from freight.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Headwinds resist; tailwinds assist. One release often names both.

concepts.caption: Forces pushing results forward.
concepts.definition: External factors that help performance: lower costs, favourable currency, strong demand.
concepts.example: Tailwinds from lower freight costs offset some of the pricing pressure.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Tailwinds assist; headwinds resist.

concepts.caption: The cash tied up just running the business day to day.
concepts.definition: Current assets minus current liabilities — the funding the operating cycle needs.
concepts.example: Working capital moved in line with the guidance the company had given.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Working capital is money tied up in operations; free cash flow is what is actually left over.

concepts.caption: What is genuinely left to spend after keeping the business running.
concepts.definition: Operating cash flow minus capital expenditure; funds dividends, buybacks and debt repayments.
concepts.example: Free cash flow of $4.1 billion covered the dividend and reduced net debt.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Free cash flow is spendable cash; working capital is cash locked in the operating cycle.

concepts.caption: The cost of keeping the lights on — it does not become an asset.
concepts.definition: Operating expenditure: day-to-day costs such as wages, rent and maintenance.
concepts.example: Operating expenditure per barrel fell 8%.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Opex is consumed and expensed now; capex becomes an asset and is depreciated over years.

concepts.caption: Big spending on plant and equipment that turns into assets.
concepts.definition: Capital expenditure on buying or upgrading long-lived assets.
concepts.example: 2026 capital expenditure of $13.5 billion to $14 billion.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Capex builds an asset; opex is expensed in the period.

concepts.caption: How much of the business is funded with borrowed money.
concepts.definition: Debt relative to equity or earnings — a measure of financial risk.
concepts.example: Leverage fell to 1.2 times net debt to EBITDA, the lowest in three years.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Leverage is a ratio; net debt is the amount that ratio is built from.

concepts.caption: Many analysts' forecasts averaged into one bar.
concepts.definition: The average of analyst estimates, the benchmark for beating or missing.
concepts.example: The company came in above the $5.11 billion consensus.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Consensus blends everyone; an estimate is one analyst's number.

concepts.caption: One specific number, usually from one analyst.
concepts.definition: An individual approximation of a value.
concepts.example: Revenue beat estimates at $21.4 billion.
concepts.mixUpWhy: An estimate can be one person's; consensus is the average of many.

concepts.caption: The reported number came in better than expected.
concepts.definition: Actual results above the market's expectation.
concepts.example: Chevron exceeded expectations, posting its strongest quarterly profit in six years.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Beat clears the bar; miss does not reach it. On results day these two words move the stock more than the numbers.

concepts.caption: The reported number fell short of expectations.
concepts.definition: Actual results below the market's expectation.
concepts.example: ExxonMobil fell short of profit projections despite a four-year earnings high.
concepts.mixUpWhy: A miss falls short; a beat clears the bar.

concepts.caption: The company's own official expectation for what comes next.
concepts.definition: Management's official outlook for future performance.
concepts.example: Capital expenditure guidance was trimmed to $9 billion.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Guidance is the company's own official number; a forecast can come from anyone about anything.

concepts.caption: An estimate of what comes next — anyone's counts.
concepts.definition: An estimate of future conditions based on current information.
concepts.example: Topping the $5.56 average analyst forecast compiled by LSEG.
concepts.mixUpWhy: A forecast is the broader idea; guidance is specifically the company's own outlook.

concepts.caption: How the company sees the trading environment ahead.
concepts.definition: Management's overall view of the next period, usually without specific numbers.
concepts.example: The outlook for the fourth quarter assumes flat pricing.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Outlook is qualitative — what conditions will be like; guidance is quantitative — what the numbers will be.

concepts.caption: Borrowed money that has to be repaid.
concepts.definition: Borrowings and bonds the company owes.
concepts.example: Free cash flow covered the dividend and reduced net debt to $12 billion.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Debt must be repaid with interest; equity is the owners' money, never repaid but it gives up ownership.

concepts.caption: The part that actually belongs to shareholders.
concepts.definition: Assets minus liabilities — the book value attributable to shareholders.
concepts.example: Return on equity improved to 14%.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Equity is the owners' residual claim; debt is a prior claim held by lenders.

concepts.caption: What is owed, minus the cash on hand.
concepts.definition: Total debt less cash and equivalents — the real burden.
concepts.example: Net debt at the end of the year stood at $8.69 billion, below target.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Net debt is an amount; leverage is that amount divided by earnings or equity.

concepts.caption: The full name of capex: money spent on long-lived assets.
concepts.definition: Spending to acquire or upgrade fixed assets, capitalised and depreciated over time.
concepts.example: Capital expenditure is set to climb by more than $1 billion next year.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Capital expenditure creates an asset; opex is consumed in the period.

concepts.caption: The collateral fell, so the lender wants more cash.
concepts.definition: A demand to top up collateral after its value falls.
concepts.example: A sharp drop in collateral values triggered margin calls across the book.
concepts.mixUpWhy: A margin call demands cash; a write-down is the company marking its own asset values down.

concepts.caption: A slice of profit paid out to shareholders.
concepts.definition: A cash or stock distribution to shareholders out of profit.
concepts.example: The firm announced a 4% dividend increase to 8.66 cents per share.
concepts.mixUpWhy: A dividend sends cash out; a buyback spends cash on its own shares, lifting the stake of everyone who stays.

concepts.caption: The company spends cash buying back its own shares.
concepts.definition: Repurchasing shares in the market, usually then cancelled, lifting earnings per share.
concepts.example: Chevron bought back $3 billion in stock during the quarter.
concepts.mixUpWhy: A buyback shrinks the share count; a dividend pays cash out.

concepts.caption: How much of its profit a company hands out.
concepts.definition: Money returned to shareholders as dividends or buybacks, or that figure as a share of profit.
concepts.example: The payout ratio stayed at 45% of earnings per share.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Payout can be a ratio or a total; a dividend is the per-share amount.

concepts.caption: What the dividend pays you at today's share price.
concepts.definition: Return relative to price; for shares, usually the dividend yield.
concepts.example: The stock yields 4.2% at the current price.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Yield is relative to the share price; payout is relative to profit. The price falls, the yield rises.

concepts.caption: Someone who owns shares in the company.
concepts.definition: A person or institution holding shares, with a residual claim and a vote.
concepts.example: Our performance has not met our shareholders' expectations.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Shareholders own shares; stakeholders also include employees, customers and lenders.

concepts.caption: The company prints new shares and sells them.
concepts.definition: Issuing new shares to raise money, diluting existing holders.
concepts.example: Share issuance funded part of the deal.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Issuance adds shares and dilutes; a buyback removes shares and concentrates.

concepts.caption: One company buys another.
concepts.definition: A transaction in which one company gains control of another.
concepts.example: Chevron realized $1.5 billion in synergies from its acquisition of Hess.
concepts.mixUpWhy: An acquisition has a buyer and a target; a merger is framed as equals combining.

concepts.caption: Two companies combine into one.
concepts.definition: Two or more companies combining into a single entity.
concepts.example: The proposed merger would create the third-largest independent producer.
concepts.mixUpWhy: A merger stresses equals combining; an acquisition stresses one party taking control.

concepts.caption: Selling off a piece of the business.
concepts.definition: The sale of a business unit or asset.
concepts.example: BP anticipates hitting $15 billion of the $20 billion divestment programme.
concepts.mixUpWhy: A divestiture usually sells for cash; a spin-off hands shareholders shares in a new listed company.

concepts.caption: A unit is separated into its own listed company.
concepts.definition: Separating a division into an independent listed company, with shares distributed to existing holders.
concepts.example: The spin-off leaves the parent focused on upstream assets.
concepts.mixUpWhy: A spin-off distributes shares, not cash; a divestiture normally sells for cash.

concepts.caption: Admitting an asset is worth less than the books say.
concepts.definition: Reducing an asset's carrying value to its recoverable amount, charging the loss to the period.
concepts.example: BP has written down more than $4 billion, largely tied to its low-carbon projects.
concepts.mixUpWhy: A write-down is the action of marking it down; impairment is the underlying loss in value.

concepts.caption: The part of an asset's value that has genuinely gone.
concepts.definition: The shortfall between an asset's recoverable amount and its carrying value, recognised as a loss.
concepts.example: Results included a $780 million impairment charge tied to a gas field.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Impairment is the fact that value fell; a write-down is recording it.

concepts.caption: Reshaping the organisation and cutting costs.
concepts.definition: A significant reorganisation of structure, portfolio or cost base, usually with one-off charges.
concepts.example: The restructuring programme will cut $400 million of annual overhead.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Restructuring changes the company from inside; a divestiture sells part of it. They often run together but are not the same.

concepts.caption: A company sells shares to the public for the first time.
concepts.definition: Initial public offering: a private company's first public share sale.
concepts.example: Dangote profits from the European fuel crunch as its IPO tests investor appetite.
concepts.mixUpWhy: An IPO is the first share sale; a listing is the state of being traded, which can happen more than once.

concepts.caption: The shares are admitted to an exchange and trade publicly.
concepts.definition: The status or act of a security being admitted to trade on an exchange.
concepts.example: Glencore shares trade higher on ASX debut after its Australian listing.
concepts.mixUpWhy: A listing is being traded on an exchange; an IPO is the first time shares are sold. A secondary listing is not an IPO.

concepts.caption: What the whole company costs on the stock market.
concepts.definition: Share price times shares outstanding — the market's total price.
concepts.example: Its market cap makes it the largest listed mining company.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Market cap is what the market pays; book value is what the accounts say the net assets are.

concepts.caption: What the company is judged to be worth.
concepts.definition: An assessment or calculation of intrinsic worth.
concepts.example: The discount reflects a lower guidance for the year ahead.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Valuation is a judgement; market cap is the price the market currently assigns.

concepts.caption: The share price as a multiple of yearly profit per share.
concepts.definition: Price divided by earnings per share — what you pay per dollar of profit.
concepts.example: On a p/e basis the shares look cheaper than peers.
concepts.mixUpWhy: P/E compares profit; P/B compares book equity. A loss-making company has no meaningful P/E but still has a P/B.

concepts.caption: The share price as a multiple of book equity per share.
concepts.definition: Price divided by book value per share, common for asset-heavy sectors.
concepts.example: Book value per share rose to $38, leaving the stock near one times book value.
concepts.mixUpWhy: P/B compares book equity; P/E compares profit. Banks and miners are read on P/B, growth companies on P/E.

concepts.caption: What the accounts say the net assets are worth.
concepts.definition: Assets minus liabilities on the balance sheet, typically at historical cost.
concepts.example: Book value per share rose to $38.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Book value is accounting net assets; market cap is the market's total price. A wide gap means the market disagrees with the books.

concepts.caption: Everyone affected by the company, not just its owners.
concepts.definition: Any party with an interest in the company: shareholders, employees, customers, suppliers, lenders.
concepts.example: Management said the restructuring would protect value for all stakeholders.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Stakeholders include everyone with an interest; shareholders are only the owners.

concepts.caption: What share of profit is handed to shareholders.
concepts.definition: Dividends divided by net profit — how generous and how sustainable the payout is.
concepts.example: The payout ratio stayed at 45% of earnings per share.
concepts.mixUpWhy: The payout ratio is a percentage; payout can also mean the total amount paid out.

concepts.caption: How much cheaper than the reference price.
concepts.definition: The extent to which a price sits below a benchmark; in valuation, the gap to peers or intrinsic value.
concepts.example: The shares trade at a discount to peers.
concepts.mixUpWhy: A discount is the market pricing it lower, which can be an opportunity; an impairment is an accounting loss because value genuinely fell.
